verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,
“Should a wise man answer with vain knowledge, and fill himself with the east wind?
Should he reason with unprofitable talk, or with speeches with which he can do no good?
Yes, you do away with fear, and hinder devotion before God.
For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the language of the crafty.
Your own mouth condemns you, and not I. Yes, your own lips testify against you.
“Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought out before the hills?
Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit wisdom to yourself?
What do you know, that we don’t know? What do you understand, which is not in us?
With us are both the gray-headed and the very aged men, much elder than your father.
Are the consolations of God too small for you, even the word that is gentle toward you?
Why does your heart carry you away? Why do your eyes flash,
That you turn your spirit against God, and let such words go out of your mouth?
What is man, that he should be clean? What is he who is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?
Behold, he puts no trust in his holy ones. Yes, the heavens are not clean in his sight;
how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks iniquity like water!
“I will show you, listen to me; that which I have seen I will declare
(which wise men have told by their fathers, and have not hidden it;
to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them):
the wicked man writhes in pain all his days, even the number of years that are laid up for the oppressor.
A sound of terrors is in his ears. In prosperity the destroyer shall come on him.
He doesn’t believe that he shall return out of darkness. He is waited for by the sword.
He wanders abroad for bread, saying, ‘Where is it?’ He knows that the day of darkness is ready at his hand.
Distress and anguish make him afraid. They prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle.
Because he has stretched out his hand against God, and behaves himself proudly against the Almighty;
he runs at him with a stiff neck, with the thick shields of his bucklers;
because he has covered his face with his fatness, and gathered fat on his thighs.
He has lived in desolate cities, in houses which no one inhabited, which were ready to become heaps.
He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue, neither shall their possessions be extended on the earth.
He shall not depart out of darkness. The flame shall dry up his branches. By the breath of God’s mouth shall he go away.
Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself; for emptiness shall be his reward.
It shall be accomplished before his time. His branch shall not be green.
He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive tree.
For the company of the godless shall be barren, and fire shall consume the tents of bribery.
They conceive mischief, and produce iniquity. Their heart prepares deceit.”

footnotes.content: Eliphaz rises to speak again—and notice how he opens not by listening but by judging. How often have I done the same in a friend's darkness, quick to words before I'd sat still long enough to hear what the Lord was doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Vain knowledge" and "east wind"—Eliphaz assumes Job speaks emptily. But here is the harder truth: sometimes the sick, not the visitors, are the ones who see clearest what is real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Unprofitable talk" mirrors an old impatience: we want our suffering explained away, not held and wept over. Eliphaz wants a problem solved; Job needs his sorrow witnessed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz says Job's words "hinder devotion before God." Gentle charge—but sometimes what looks like false confidence is actually true complaint offered honestly into God's ear, which is its own kind of prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your iniquity teaches your mouth." Eliphaz is certain: Job's words are proof of hidden sin. Yet the Lord later rebukes Eliphaz, not Job. This is the danger of being too sure we know why someone suffers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your own mouth condemns you." A legal image—Job's words as witnesses against him. But I've learned the Lord hears the cry beneath the words, not only the words themselves. Our deepest plea may sound like blame until grace translates it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Were you born before the hills?" Sarcasm: You presume knowledge you don't possess. Yet Eliphaz, too, presumes—to know exactly why Job suffers and what it means. Pride wears many faces.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Have you heard the secret counsel of God?" A question that assumes the answer is no. But the irony is that Job, in his rawness, is listening. The Lord will respond to him directly before the dialogue ends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What do you know that we don't know?" The friends form a chorus of certainty. How many have I joined such choirs, where the noise of agreement drowns out the voice asking for help?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz leans on age: "gray-headed and very aged men." Older years can bring wisdom, yes—but also weariness, and the temptation to make quick judgments about suffering we haven't lately tasted ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Are the consolations of God too small for you?" The friends believe they are offering God's comfort; Job hears their words as stones. Comfort forced on the grieving often wounds instead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why does your heart carry you away? Why do your eyes flash?" Eliphaz reads Job's passion as rebellion. But I've come to see that fire in the eye can be the heat of a soul wrestling with the Lord, which is sometimes more honest than calm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You turn your spirit against God." Here is the charge made plain: Job is faithless. Yet faith is not the absence of hard questions—sometimes it is the courage to ask them before the throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What is man, that he should be clean?" A humbling truth—we are all mixed, all flawed. Yet Eliphaz uses this to accuse Job. In our own mouths, the same words about human weakness become either grace or judgment, depending on whom we speak to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He puts no trust in his holy ones." Even the heavens lack purity in God's sight. This is orthodox—and utterly unhelpful to someone in agony. Sometimes the most correct theology becomes cruelty when delivered without tears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "One who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks iniquity like water." The language is vicious. Job never said such things of himself. Eliphaz supplies the harshness, the damnation, for his friend. This is what judgment looks like dressed as diagnosis.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will show you; listen to me." Eliphaz shifts into his main argument, speaking with authority. But authority without empathy is mere dominance wearing the mask of truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Wise men have told their fathers" and "the land was given" to them alone. Eliphaz grounds his argument in tradition and heritage. Wisdom passed down through generations carries weight—yet without the Spirit to renew it, even ancient words grow brittle and hard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The wicked man writhes in pain all his days." Eliphaz's thesis: suffering = wickedness. But the Lord will later reject this equation as a lie. Not every pain is punishment; sometimes it is testing, or mystery, or the cost of love in a broken world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "A sound of terrors in his ears." The enemies of the wicked are ever near. Eliphaz paints a picture of endless dread as the wage of sin. Yet sometimes terror comes to the faithful too, and peace to the undeserving.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He doesn't believe he shall return out of darkness." Hopelessness becomes proof of guilt in Eliphaz's logic. But despair is not always a symptom of sin—sometimes it is the honest face of grief before grace meets us there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He wanders abroad for bread, saying, 'Where is it?'" The portrait of a man undone, cast out, hungry. Eliphaz speaks as though describing a stranger—yet his words are meant to fit Job like a shroud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Distress and anguish make him afraid. They prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle." Warfare language—the suffering man is embattled, hemmed in. Eliphaz means it as verdict; it is also simply the human truth of severe loss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He has stretched out his hand against God, and behaves proudly against the Almighty." Pride and rebellion are the charges. Yet sometimes what looks like rebellion is a child shaking his fist at a Father whose face feels turned away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He runs at him with a stiff neck, with thick shields of his bucklers." Battle-speak continues. Eliphaz is convinced of the wicked man's defiance. But I've learned that sometimes a rigid neck is just a man braced against collapse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He has covered his face with his fatness, and gathered fat on his thighs." A peculiar touch—Eliphaz mocks the wicked man's self-indulgence. Yet shame often wears the face of excess. We harden ourselves with whatever we can grab.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He has lived in desolate cities, in houses which no one inhabited." A portrait of isolation and abandonment. Is this punishment for sin, or simply the geography of suffering—the way it leaves us alone, even when friends sit nearby?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue." Eliphaz piles on material poverty as part of the divine sentence. Yet I have seen the wealthy destroyed and the destitute upheld by invisible hands. God's economy is not so simple.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He shall not depart out of darkness. The flame shall dry up his branches." Eliphaz's portrait culminates in total destruction—no escape, no green thing, only drought and fire. Yet the story of the faithful also moves through fire. The furnace does not always mean damnation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself." A warning: the deceived does not know his own deception. How many have I warned others with these words, certain I could see their folly—while missing my own?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "It shall be accomplished before his time. His branch shall not be green." The wicked are cut short, unnaturally young in their ruin. Eliphaz speaks of divine pruning as judgment. Yet the innocent also wither sometimes, and the wicked prosper to gray hair.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive tree." Images of a harvest ruined before it ripens. Eliphaz uses harvest language—fruitlessness as the wicked man's fate. Yet the Lord brings forth fruit through seasons we do not choose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The company of the godless shall be barren, and fire shall consume the tents of bribery." Eliphaz draws his great circle: godlessness breeds emptiness; corruption invites burning. This is coherent theology—but it does not answer Job.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They conceive mischief, and produce iniquity. Their heart prepares deceit." Eliphaz closes his harsh words—and yet listeners today hear an echo: these same words describe the friends themselves, who have conceived a cruel judgment and birthed it with such certainty. The Lord will later require them to repent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
